primary_activity.atb: ATB (All Terrain Biking) — Gravel, Cyclocross, etc.

evc/moped.name: Moped, up to 2 hp and 30 mph
evc/moped.description: The moped the classifications naming this group share: a motor of no more than 2 brake horsepower (1,492 W) that can't propel it faster than 30 mph. A vehicle carries this group's id in place of each classification in it.
restrictions: Its motor produces no more than 2 brake horsepower (1,492 W)
The motor can't propel it faster than 30 mph
Past its jurisdiction's e-bike limits; one within them is an electric bicycle instead
Each classification naming this group holds its own jurisdiction's license, registration, insurance, helmet and riding rules

evc/motor_driven_cycle.name: Motor-Driven Cycle, up to 5 hp
evc/motor_driven_cycle.description: The motor-driven cycle the classifications naming this group share: a motorcycle whose motor produces no more than 5 brake horsepower (3,730 W). A vehicle carries this group's id in place of each classification in it.
restrictions: A seat or saddle and no more than three wheels
Its motor produces no more than 5 brake horsepower (3,730 W)
Past its jurisdiction's e-bike limits, and its moped's where the jurisdiction has one
Each classification naming this group holds its own jurisdiction's license, registration, insurance, helmet and riding rules

evc/motorcycle.name: Motorcycle, over 5 hp
evc/motorcycle.description: A road motorcycle whose motor produces more than 5 brake horsepower (3,730 W), which is a motorcycle under every classification naming this group. A vehicle carries this group's id in place of each classification in it.
restrictions: A seat or saddle and no more than three wheels
Its motor produces more than 5 brake horsepower (3,730 W)
Built for highway use; one built for off-highway use is an off-highway motorcycle instead
Each classification naming this group holds its own jurisdiction's license, registration, insurance, helmet and riding rules

evc/off_highway_motorcycle.name: Off-Highway Motorcycle
evc/off_highway_motorcycle.description: An electric motorcycle built for off-highway use, such as an electric dirt bike, ridden under the off-highway category of each classification naming this group. A vehicle carries this group's id in place of each classification in it.
restrictions: Built by its manufacturer for off-highway use, not for the road
No limit on motor power or speed
Kept off public roads except where its jurisdiction allows it
Each classification naming this group holds its own jurisdiction's license, registration, insurance, helmet and riding rules

evc/us/ca/moped.name: Moped
evc/us/ca/moped.description: A moped or motorized bicycle: two or three wheels, a motor under 4 gross brake horsepower (3,000 W), and a top speed of 30 mph on level ground. Defined by California Vehicle Code §406, as amended by SB 1167 (Chapter 846, Statutes of 2026).
restrictions: Two or three wheels and an automatic transmission; pedals are optional
Its motor produces less than 4 gross brake horsepower (3,000 W)
Can't propel it faster than 30 mph on level ground
Built for highway use: meets federal motor vehicle safety standards, with a 17-digit VIN and a safety certification label
Riders need a driver's license with an M1 or M2 motorcycle endorsement, so must be 16 or older
Riders must wear a motorcycle helmet
Registered with the DMV and carries a moped plate; registering it doesn't require insurance
Barred from any freeway or expressway where Caltrans or the local authority posts a prohibition
Kept off bike paths and trails unless they run beside a roadway or a local ordinance allows it
A vehicle, not property: it can be towed or impounded

evc/us/ca/motor_driven_cycle.name: Motor-driven cycle
evc/us/ca/motor_driven_cycle.description: A light electric motorcycle: its motor produces 5 gross brake horsepower (3,750 W) or less, the electric counterpart of a motorcycle under 150 cc. Defined by California Vehicle Code §405, as amended by SB 1167 (Chapter 846, Statutes of 2026).
restrictions: A motorcycle: a seat or saddle, and no more than three wheels on the ground
Its motor produces 5 gross brake horsepower (3,750 W) or less; one under 3,000 W is a motor-driven cycle rather than a moped when it can go faster than 30 mph
Built for highway use: meets federal motor vehicle safety standards, with a 17-digit VIN and a safety certification label
Riders need a driver's license with an M1 motorcycle endorsement
Riders must wear a motorcycle helmet
Registered and plated with the DMV, and must carry liability insurance
Barred from any freeway or expressway where Caltrans or the local authority posts a prohibition
Not allowed on bike paths or trails
A vehicle, not property: it can be towed or impounded

evc/us/ca/motorcycle.name: Motorcycle
evc/us/ca/motorcycle.description: A road-registered electric motorcycle: its motor produces more than 5 gross brake horsepower (3,750 W), above what a motor-driven cycle may. Defined by California Vehicle Code §400, with the line set by SB 1167 (Chapter 846, Statutes of 2026).
restrictions: A seat or saddle, and no more than three wheels on the ground
Its motor produces more than 5 gross brake horsepower (3,750 W)
Built for highway use: meets federal motor vehicle safety standards, with a 17-digit VIN and a safety certification label; one built for off-highway use is an off-highway electric motorcycle instead
Riders need a driver's license with an M1 motorcycle endorsement
Riders must wear a motorcycle helmet
Registered and plated with the DMV, and must carry liability insurance
Allowed on freeways
Not allowed on bike paths or trails
A vehicle, not property: it can be towed or impounded

evc/us/ca/off_highway_electric_motorcycl.name: Off-highway electric motorcycle
evc/us/ca/off_highway_electric_motorcycl.description: An electric motorcycle built for riding off the highway, an "eMoto": two wheels, handlebars, a straddle seat and no pedals from the manufacturer, with no limit on power or speed. Defined by California Vehicle Code §436.1, added by SB 586 (2025).
restrictions: Designed by the manufacturer primarily for off-highway use, with two wheels, handlebars, a straddle seat and no pedals from the manufacturer
No limit on motor power or speed
Not an electric bicycle or moped, whatever its power, and can't be sold or labeled as an electric bicycle; adding pedals doesn't make it one
Identified with a California OHV Green Sticker from the DMV to ride on public lands, or on private land open to the public
Ridden only in designated OHV areas or on private property; never on highways, streets, sidewalks, bike lanes or bike paths
Can't be registered or converted for street use
No driver's license needed off the highway; riding it on a highway is unregistered, unlicensed operation

evc/us/ca/off_highway_motor_vehicle.name: Off-highway motor vehicle
evc/us/ca/off_highway_motor_vehicle.description: A motor vehicle used only off the highway and not registered for it, such as an electric ATV or off-road quad. Defined by California Vehicle Code §38010 and §38012, whose list of examples (all-terrain vehicles, dirt bikes, dune buggies, jeeps) isn't exhaustive.
restrictions: Not registered for highway use, so it can't be ridden on a highway, street, sidewalk, bike lane or bike path
Ridden only in designated OHV areas, on public lands open to off-highway vehicles, or on private property
Identified with a California OHV Green Sticker from the DMV to ride on public lands, or on private land open to the public; not needed on private land the owner controls

One that is an all-terrain vehicle (a single seat the operator straddles, three or more low-pressure tires, 50 inches or narrower and 900 lb or lighter) also needs: a motorcycle helmet on everyone aboard, a safety certificate, training course or certified adult's supervision for a rider under 18, a parent or authorized adult supervising a rider under 14, and no passenger unless it's built for one

evc/us/class_1.name: Class 1
evc/us/class_1.description: A pedal-assist electric bicycle: the motor helps only while the rider pedals, and stops helping at 20 mph. Defined by the three-class model law most states have adopted; state and local rules can add to these.
restrictions: Fully operable pedals, a saddle or seat, and a motor of less than 750 watts
No throttle: the motor assists only while the rider is pedaling
The motor stops assisting at 20 mph, and disengages when the rider stops pedaling or applies the brakes
Carries a permanent label stating its class, top assisted speed and motor wattage
Must not be modified to change its motor-powered speed or engagement unless the label is replaced to match
Meets the CPSC's bicycle requirements (16 CFR part 1512)
Ridden wherever bicycles are allowed, including streets, bike lanes and bicycle or multi-use paths
A local authority may ban it from a bicycle or multi-use path only after notice and a public hearing, for safety or legal reasons
On a natural-surface trail designated nonmotorized, the agency that manages the trail decides whether it's allowed
Treated as a bicycle, not a motor vehicle: no driver's license, registration or insurance

evc/us/class_2.name: Class 2
evc/us/class_2.description: A throttle electric bicycle: the motor can propel it without pedaling, and stops helping at 20 mph, by throttle or by pedal assist. Defined by the three-class model law most states have adopted; state and local rules can add to these.
restrictions: Fully operable pedals, a saddle or seat, and a motor of less than 750 watts
The motor may propel it on its own, with a throttle, but can't assist at all at 20 mph or faster
The motor disengages when the brakes are applied
Carries a permanent label stating its class, top assisted speed and motor wattage
Must not be modified to change its motor-powered speed or engagement unless the label is replaced to match
Meets the CPSC's bicycle requirements (16 CFR part 1512)
Ridden wherever bicycles are allowed, including streets, bike lanes and bicycle or multi-use paths
A local authority may ban it from a bicycle or multi-use path only after notice and a public hearing, for safety or legal reasons
On a natural-surface trail designated nonmotorized, the agency that manages the trail decides whether it's allowed
Treated as a bicycle, not a motor vehicle: no driver's license, registration or insurance

evc/us/class_3.name: Class 3
evc/us/class_3.description: A speed pedal-assist electric bicycle: the motor helps only while the rider pedals, and stops helping at 28 mph. Defined by the three-class model law most states have adopted; state and local rules can add to these.
restrictions: Fully operable pedals, a saddle or seat, and a motor of less than 750 watts
No throttle: the motor assists only while the rider is pedaling
The motor stops assisting at 28 mph, and disengages when the rider stops pedaling or applies the brakes
Must have a speedometer showing its speed in miles per hour
Riders must be 16 or older; a younger passenger may ride on one designed to carry passengers
Riders and passengers must wear a bicycle helmet meeting CPSC or ASTM standards
Carries a permanent label stating its class, top assisted speed and motor wattage
Must not be modified to change its motor-powered speed or engagement unless the label is replaced to match
Meets the CPSC's bicycle requirements (16 CFR part 1512)

A local authority may ban it from any bicycle or multi-use path, with no hearing needed; some states, California among them, keep it off paths and trails unless they run beside a roadway or a local ordinance allows it
On a natural-surface trail designated nonmotorized, the agency that manages the trail decides whether it's allowed
Treated as a bicycle, not a motor vehicle: no driver's license, registration or insurance

evc/us/co/electric_bicycle.name: Electrical Assisted Bicycle
evc/us/co/electric_bicycle.description: A vehicle with two or three wheels, fully operable pedals and an electric motor of no more than 750 watts, in one of three classes: Class 1 pedal assist to 20 mph, Class 2 throttle to 20 mph, and Class 3 pedal assist to 28 mph. Defined by Colorado Revised Statutes §42-1-102(28.5), as amended by HB 25-1197 (2025), and regulated by §§42-4-221 and 42-4-1412.
restrictions: Class 1 and Class 3 assist only while the rider pedals, cutting out at 20 and 28 mph; Class 2 may assist without pedaling, to 20 mph
Class 1 and 3 need a cutoff that can't be bypassed, stopping the motor when the rider stops pedaling; a Class 2 motor stops when the brakes are applied
A vehicle modified out of every class, or built to be easily switched out of one by a button, setting or app, is not an electrical assisted bicycle
A multiple-mode e-bike that can switch between classes must meet the rules of each class it can run as, and from January 1, 2027 its label must name those classes

Carries a permanent label, in Arial at least 9-point, stating its class, top assisted speed and motor wattage, and must not be modified to change its speed or motor engagement unless the label is replaced to match
Sellers must disclose its wattage, top speed and class; selling a vehicle that isn't one as an e-bike without a written disclosure is a deceptive trade practice
Its lithium-ion battery must be certified by an accredited lab to a UL 2849 or EN 15194 battery standard
Meets the CPSC's bicycle requirements (16 CFR part 1512)
Class 3 riders must be 16 or older; a younger passenger may ride on one designed to carry passengers
Class 3 riders and passengers under 18 must wear a bicycle helmet meeting CPSC or ASTM standards, and a Class 3 must have a speedometer
Class 1 and Class 2 may ride bike and pedestrian paths where bicycles are allowed, but a local authority may ban them from its paths
Class 3 is kept off bike and pedestrian paths unless the path is within a street or highway or the local authority allows it
On a sidewalk it yields to pedestrians, and local ordinances or signs may ban it there
In state parks, Class 1 and 2 may ride roads, bike lanes and trails open to bicycles; in state wildlife areas, e-bikes are limited to roads and camping or parking areas open to motor vehicles
Its rider has the same rights and duties as a bicyclist, and it is not a motor vehicle: no registration or driver's license

evc/us/in/electric_bicycle.name: Electric Bicycle
evc/us/in/electric_bicycle.description: A bicycle with operable pedals and an electric motor with a power output of no more than 750 watts, in one of three classes: Class 1 and Class 3 pedal-assist up to 20 and 28 mph, and Class 2 throttle-assisted up to 20 mph. Defined by Indiana Code §9-13-2-49.2 and regulated by §9-21-11-13.1, as enacted by HEA 1236 (2019).
restrictions: A bicycle with operable pedals and a motor with a power output of no more than 750 watts
Class 1 assists only while the rider pedals and stops at 20 mph; Class 2 can be throttle-propelled up to 20 mph; Class 3 assists only while pedaling and stops at 28 mph
The motor must disengage or stop assisting when the rider stops pedaling or applies the brakes
Meets the CPSC's bicycle requirements (16 CFR part 1512)
Carries a permanent label stating its class, top assisted speed and motor wattage; anyone who modifies its speed or motor engagement must update the label
Class 3 riders must be 15 or older; a younger passenger may ride on one designed to carry passengers
Class 3 riders and passengers under 18 must wear a bicycle helmet meeting CPSC or ASTM standards
Regulated as a bicycle, with a bicycle rider's rights and duties, and may be ridden wherever bicycles may
Class 1 and Class 2 may use bicycle and multipurpose paths open to bicycles unless a statute, rule or local ordinance says otherwise
Class 3 is kept off bicycle and multipurpose paths unless the path runs within or beside a highway or the local authority or state agency in charge allows it
On a natural-surface trail designated nonmotorized, the local authority or state agency that manages it decides which classes are allowed
On DNR properties all classes may use roads, Class 1 and Class 2 may use paved and gravel trails, and only Class 1 may use natural-surface trails open to bicycles
Not a motor vehicle: no driver's license, title, registration or insurance, and exempt from off-road vehicle rules

evc/us/nj/electric_bicycle.name: Low-Speed Electric Bicycle
evc/us/nj/electric_bicycle.description: A two-wheeled bicycle with fully operable pedals and an electric motor that helps only while the rider pedals and stops helping at 20 mph. P.L.2025, c.285 (S4834, signed January 19, 2026) narrowed it to pedal assist, moved throttle and 28 mph e-bikes into the motorized bicycle category, and made riders of both license and register them. Defined by N.J.S.A. 39:1-1 and regulated by N.J.S.A. 39:4-14.16 and 39:4-14.3i.
restrictions: Two wheels and fully operable pedals; the motor assists only while the rider is pedaling and stops assisting at 20 mph
The definition sets no motor wattage limit

An e-bike with a throttle, or with pedal assist past 20 mph up to 28 mph, is a motorized bicycle instead: it also needs a license and registration, must carry liability insurance, and is barred from roads posted over 50 mph
One with pedals and a motor over 750 watts that can exceed 28 mph is an electric motorized bicycle, which the law counts as a motorcycle
Riders must be 15 or older
Riders need a driver's license or a motorized bicycle (e-bike) license from the Motor Vehicle Commission, which takes a knowledge test and a road test; 15- and 16-year-olds need the e-bike license
Registered with the Motor Vehicle Commission, with its two plate stickers displayed on the front fork; required since July 19, 2026, after a six-month grace period
No insurance required
Riders under 17 must wear a bicycle helmet
Ridden on streets, highways and bicycle paths; a county or municipality may ban it from bicycle paths it controls
May be parked on a sidewalk if it doesn't block pedestrians
Kept off natural-surface trails designated non-motorized unless the local authority allows it
Selling a kit that converts it into a motorized or electric motorized bicycle is prohibited
Not a motor vehicle; the laws that apply to bicycles otherwise apply to it
A bike-share rider 16 or older needs no license, and the rider doesn't register a shared e-bike

evc/us/ny/electric_bicycle.name: Bicycle With Electric Assist
evc/us/ny/electric_bicycle.description: A bicycle no more than 36 inches wide, with operable pedals and an electric motor of less than 750 watts, in one of three classes: class 1 pedal assist and class 2 throttle, both to 20 mph, and class 3, which may run on the motor alone to 25 mph and is allowed only in a city of a million or more people. Defined by Vehicle and Traffic Law §102-c and regulated by §1242.
restrictions: No more than 36 inches wide, with operable pedals and an electric motor of less than 750 watts
Class 1 assists only while the rider is pedaling and class 2 may be propelled by the motor alone; both stop assisting at 20 mph
Class 3 may be propelled by the motor alone and stops assisting at 25 mph; it may be ridden only in a city of a million or more people, which means New York City
Meets the CPSC's bicycle requirements (16 CFR part 1512)
Carries a label stating its class, top assisted speed and motor wattage, required since June 1, 2022
Riders must be 16 or older
Class 3 riders must wear a helmet
Not registered with the DMV
State law allows it on roads with a posted speed limit of 30 mph or less and in bicycle lanes
Not ridden on a sidewalk unless a local law allows it; may be parked on one if it leaves pedestrians room to pass
Cities, towns and villages may further regulate when, where and how it's ridden, including speed limits, helmets and reflective gear; New York City has capped e-bikes at 15 mph since October 24, 2025
On public lands other than roads it may be ridden only where the agency in charge authorizes it

State parks allow class 1 and class 2 on boardwalks and paved or improved paths at up to 15 mph, and class 1 alone on natural-surface trails open to bicycles; class 3 is banned at every state park facility, and all classes from parkways
Breaking these rules carries a civil fine of up to $50

evc/us/tx/electric_bicycle.name: Electric Bicycle
evc/us/tx/electric_bicycle.description: A bicycle with fully operable pedals and an electric motor of fewer than 750 watts, with a top assisted speed of 28 mph or less, in one of three classes: Class 1 pedal assist to 20 mph, Class 2 throttle to 20 mph, and Class 3 pedal assist to 28 mph. Defined by Texas Transportation Code §664.001 and regulated by §§551.106–551.107, both added by HB 2188 (2019).
restrictions: Fully operable pedals and an electric motor of fewer than 750 watts, with a top assisted speed of 28 mph or less
Class 1 assists only while the rider pedals, to a top assisted speed of 20 mph
Class 2 can be propelled by its motor without pedaling, to a top assisted speed of 20 mph
Class 3 assists only while the rider pedals, to a top assisted speed of more than 20 but less than 28 mph, and must be sold with a speedometer
May only be ridden if the motor disengages when the rider stops pedaling or applies the brakes
Carries a permanent label stating its class, top assisted speed and motor wattage; anyone who changes its motor-powered speed or engagement must replace the label to match
Meets the CPSC's bicycle requirements (16 CFR part 1512)
Class 3 riders must be 15 or older; a younger passenger may ride on one
No statewide helmet requirement
No driver's license, title or insurance, and it can't be registered for highway use
TxDOT and local authorities may not ban it from roads used mainly by motor vehicles, or from anywhere a regular bicycle may go, except natural-surface trails closed to motor vehicles
TxDOT and local authorities may ban bicycles, e-bikes included, from sidewalks and set speed limits on bicycle paths

evc/us/tx/off_highway_motorcycle.name: Off-Highway Motorcycle
evc/us/tx/off_highway_motorcycle.description: A motorcycle ridden for off-highway recreation, one of the off-highway vehicles that need a Texas Parks and Wildlife decal on public riding land, which is how an off-road electric dirt bike is ridden legally. Defined as an off-highway vehicle by Texas Parks and Wildlife Code §29.001.
restrictions: Built for off-highway recreation; no limit on motor power or speed

Needs an annual off-highway vehicle decal from Texas Parks and Wildlife, at least $8 and valid September through August, to ride on public land or land developed with a department grant where off-highway riding is legal

The Transportation Code calls a seated two-wheeler with an electric motor that isn't designed for highway use and can't be titled a pocket bike or minimotorbike, and nothing in Texas's scooter law authorizes one on a road, street, bicycle path or sidewalk
The all-terrain vehicle rules, including their safety certificate, cover only vehicles on three or more tires

175.description: 10in (60/65-6.9) Segway Ninebot Max G2, E2 Pro, E3, F3 e-scooters (Uncommon)

191.description: 11in (7.5in rim) Segway GT3, Max G3 e-scooters (Uncommon)

483.description: 19in motorcycle rim (70/100-19) Sur-Ron Light Bee X, Ultra Bee, Segway Xaber e-motos (Uncommon)

520.description: 24 x 1 performance wheels for smaller riders (Uncommon)

571.description: 650 C, Schwinn Cruisers, Tri- and Time-trial bikes (uncommon)

584.description: 650 B, 27.5 mountain bikes, smaller road bikes (Standard size)
